Senses.Explanation: “The mortar pounds, the mill grinds” is a paired work image used as a compact answer and as a description of activity that follows its fixed conditions. Baiyun Shouduan gives the pair as an answer when a monk says there is nowhere to lodge. Dahui Zonggao applies it to what does not fail someone who has actually gained entry. Yuanjie Jingying lists it among the consequences of having a direction or dependence, while Pinjixiang Zhixiang places it in an instruction about revealing the teaching body.
Senses.Note: Keep the two work actions together. The directional expansions “the mortar pounds southeast” and “the mill pushes northwest” are fuller phrases, not substitutes for this headword.

Senses.Explanation: Huike's fixed reply in the mind-settling case. Huike says his mind is not at ease; Bodhidharma tells him to bring the mind so it can be set at ease; Huike answers, ‘having sought the mind, I could not find it’; Bodhidharma replies that the mind has now been set at ease. Yuanwu asks why Huike answered only this. Juelang distinguishes Huike’s utterance from later students repeating it. Zhuanyu Guanheng judges the reply as conceptual understanding. Daxiu Zhu reuses it in a first-person question, and Wanfeng asks how it should be understood. These uses concern one fixed quoted reply.

At an opening-of-the-brazier sermon Poshan Haiming calls the whole earth a furnace and asks where its smoke comes from. He rejects answers based on birth and death, transcendence, afflictions or pride, then urges sustained work with delusion and awakening until fixed views fall away. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB177.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Poshan. At an opening-of-the-brazier sermon Poshan Haiming calls the whole earth a furnace and asks where its smoke comes from. He rejects answers based on birth and death, transcendence, afflictions or pride, then urges sustained work with delusion and awakening until fixed views fall away. Striking his staff, he asks whether the audience understands and gives the fire-and-water couplet. The line is Poshan's present answer to his furnace and smoke challenge, not a separate promise of hidden fire.

Senses.Explanation: The paired images find smoke with fire and the moon with water carried home. Masters use them as a complete response to a challenge about what lies at hand, including Tianyin's proposed answer to Fenyang and several later hall questions. Tianyin Yuanxiu recalls an older challenge by Fenyang, who was picking chrysanthemums and asked the assembly for one fitting line without harming the things named. Tianyin says that if he, as a distant descendant, had been present, he would have answered with seeking fire amid smoke and carrying spring water home with the moon. He then works through Fenyang's further guest-and-host sayings and tests his own assembly with staff gestures. The selected couplet is Tianyin's proposed present answer to the older challenge, not a line spoken by Fenyang. In a hall address connected to a question about commending a deceased father, Linwo Jian answers the monk's initial question and two follow-up questions, striking him when asked about turning around. He then warns against clever remaking of the world and against pausing at appearances, asks whether the assembly understands, and closes with the fire-and-water couplet before leaving the seat. Linwo speaks the line as his own conclusion to this service address; the earlier questions are asked by the monk. At an opening-of-the-brazier sermon Poshan Haiming calls the whole earth a furnace and asks where its smoke comes from. He rejects answers based on birth and death, transcendence, afflictions or pride, then urges sustained work with delusion and awakening until fixed views fall away. Striking his staff, he asks whether the audience understands and gives the fire-and-water couplet. The line is Poshan's present answer to his furnace and smoke challenge, not a separate promise of hidden fire. Ruibai Mingxue opens a hall sermon with autumn leaves, passing clouds, a clear wisdom mirror and ancestral teaching, asks whether the assembly understands, and gives the fire-and-water couplet. He then explains that layman Xing Jixian has provided a meal to celebrate Ruibai's birthday and requested a teaching that forms a wisdom connection, after which Ruibai wishes the donor progress and poses another question. The couplet belongs to Ruibai's own introductory sermon; the donor is its occasion, not its speaker. Yunhuan Yinchen tells his assembly that everyone has the seed of awakening. He says that one speck enters right reception while complete command arises in all specks, raises his whisk, and asks for a line when guest and host are merged. He answers with the fire-and-water couplet. Yunhuan voices it as the present response to his own guest-and-host challenge, with the concrete images carrying the turn rather than naming a new physical journey. The word means a cat. Its most heavily transmitted Zen deployment is the public case in which the eastern and western halls fight over a cat: Nanquan lifts it and says, "if you can speak, I will not cut it; if you cannot speak, I will cut it" (道得即不斬，道不得即斬卻). The assembly does not answer and the record says he cuts it; when Zhaozhou returns, he puts a straw sandal on his head, and Nanquan says he would have saved the cat. Later teachers repeatedly ask about, title, verse, and comment on "Nanquan cuts the cat" (南泉斬貓). The same word also retains its ordinary animal use, including a cat's fixed attention while catching a mouse.
Senses.Note: Later Chan records explicitly debate the killing rather than silently resolving it. One late account says one hall cited a rule that "the bodhisattva precepts do not permit keeping cats, foxes, pigs, and dogs" (菩薩戒中不許長養貓狸豬狗), while the other wanted the cat to control mice; that speaker later calls the killing a sin. Another transmitted verdict answers the question about the case with only "it takes a Nanquan" (須是南泉始得). These are attested later deployments; this entry does not project their precept explanation backward as the early record's stated intent. The simplified spelling of “cat” is a separate searchable entry but not a different meaning.

Entries.SourceTerm: 貓有歃血之功，虎有起屍之德

Senses.PreferredTarget: The cat has the power to lap blood; the tiger has the power to stir the dead
SearchAliases: the cat has the power to lap blood; the tiger has the power to stir the dead
Senses.Note: The unusual pair gives a cat the work of lapping blood and a tiger the power to stir the dead. Wanru puts it beside contrasts between hearer and bodhisattva. Feiyin applies it to officers whose work must actually help the community. Guantao follows it with an impossible moving temple, while Huiyue says a teacher’s word can bring a deadened student back to life. Yushan gives the pair as a direct reply. These turns use the images for force in action, not as a report about animal habits.

Senses.Explanation: Not even a hair can fit between: the phrase denies the smallest interval in the relation named by each case. Zhongfeng says awakened clarity and ordinary applications admit no intervening hair; Dahui places the phrase between one thought and its application; Xueyan compares the meeting to two mirrors with no hair admitted; Xieyun uses it for a house rule whose exacting edge leaves no gap.
